Juvenile Potomida littoralis emerge from their benthic egg masses as glochidia larvae at a water temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C], with the hatching event occurring approximately 10 days [ab = approximately 10 days] after egg deposition. This duration is relatively brief for a freshwater mussel, reflecting a strategy that prioritizes rapid entry into the parasitic phase. Following a period of host attachment, the larvae undergo metamorphosis and subsequently settle out of the water column as tiny post-larval individuals. At the moment of settlement, the shell length of these newly metamorphosed juveniles is approximately 0.03 cm , a size that makes them highly vulnerable to predation and physical disturbance. The initial shell length at birth, recorded as 0.02 cm [Lb = 0.02 cm], indicates that the glochidium stage itself is exceptionally small, representing the earliest measurable size in the species' life cycle. These minute dimensions underscore the considerable challenges faced during the early post-settlement period, when survivorship is notoriously low among unionid bivalves.

Data from mark-recapture studies and growth ring analyses indicate that Potomida littoralis is a relatively long-lived species, with a maximum recorded lifespan of approximately 29,200 days [am = approximately 29,200 days] when maintained at a stable temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. This longevity, spanning roughly eight decades, is a characteristic shared with other large-bodied freshwater mussels. Individuals exhibit continuous, albeit decelerating, growth throughout their adult years. The ultimate shell length is estimated to approach 10 cm [Li = 10 cm], a size that can be attained after several decades of sustained somatic growth. The asymptotic dry tissue mass, corrected for shell size, reaches approximately 36 grams [Wwi = approximately 36 grams]. This substantial body mass supports a high fecundity, as larger females are capable of brooding a greater number of larvae within their marsupial gills. The extreme longevity, in conjunction with a large body size, positions P. littoralis as a dominant competitor for space and resources within its benthic habitat.

Reproductive maturity in Potomida littoralis is not attained until the shell reaches a specific morphological threshold. Analysis of size-at-age data, informed by estimated growth curves, suggests that puberty occurs when the shell length reaches approximately 1.2 cm [Lp = approximately 1.2 cm]. This size, corresponding to an age of roughly 4 to 5 years, marks the onset of gametogenesis and the development of functional gonads. Prior to this size, individuals are considered sexually immature and allocate resources exclusively to growth and somatic maintenance. The attainment of this critical shell length is a necessary precondition for entering the breeding population. Achieving this size threshold signifies a major life-history transition from a strictly somatic growth phase to one capable of both continued growth and reproductive investment. Consequently, juvenile survival up to this size is a key demographic bottleneck.

During the active reproductive season, gravid females release glochidia larvae. The maximum reproductive rate for this species has been estimated under controlled laboratory conditions at 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, females have been observed to produce approximately 274 larvae per day [Ri = approximately 274 larvae per day], which over the course of a single breeding season constitutes a substantial investment in offspring. This value, derived from empirical counts of expelled glochidia, is among the highest recorded for European unionid mussels. The high fecundity partially compensates for the extremely low survival rates experienced during the parasitic larval stage and the vulnerable post-settlement juvenile phase. The timing of this reproductive output is closely tied to water temperature, with spawning events becoming more frequent and voluminous as temperatures rise during the late spring and early summer months. This continuous release throughout the spawning period means that each female participates in multiple spawning events per season, effectively producing numerous reproductive events annually to maximize the probability of successful host infestation.

The life-history strategy of Potomida littoralis can be understood as a classic equilibrium or bet-hedging approach. Very few of the estimated 274 larvae released daily [Ri = 274 larvae released daily] survive to adulthood, given the extreme mortality bottlenecks at settlement. The species compensates for this high early mortality not by accelerating maturation, but by attaining a very large maximum shell length of approximately 10 cm [Li = approximately 10 cm] and an ultimate dry weight of approximately 36 grams [Wwi = approximately 36 grams], which together support immense lifetime fecundity. The observed lifespan of 29,200 days [am = 29,200 days] at 14 °C [T = 14 °C] further amplifies the total number of reproductive events over an individual's lifetime. Furthermore, the minute size of the larvae at birth (0.02 cm [Lb = 0.02 cm] shell length) and at settlement (0.03 cm ) necessitates an extended parasitic phase to reach a size capable of independent benthic life. This suite of traits, including late maturity at 1.2 cm [Lp = 1.2 cm] shell length and a prolonged lifespan, is typical of a slow-paced, highly resilient species inhabiting stable, predictable riverine environments.
